passages.t: A message to Hiram of Tyre
passages.happening:
When Hiram king of Tyre hears that Solomon has been anointed king, he sends envoys, ‘for Hiram had always been a friend of David’ (verse 1).

Solomon sends back a message. His father could not build a house for the Name of the LORD because of the wars on every side. “But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side, and there is no adversary or crisis” (verse 4). So Solomon plans to build it, as the LORD told David: “I will put your son on your throne in your place, and he will build the house for My Name” (verse 5).

He asks Hiram to have cedars of Lebanon cut for him. His servants will work with Hiram's, and he will pay whatever wages Hiram sets, ‘for you know that there are none among us as skilled in logging as the Sidonians’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The whole story of David's house has been moving toward this. David wanted to build a house for God, and God answered through Nathan that David's son would build it, while God would build David a house, a line of kings. Solomon now quotes that promise and acts on it.

Tyre was the leading city of the Phoenicians, a seafaring people on the coast of what is now Lebanon, famous for trade, shipbuilding and skilled work. Hiram is known outside the Bible too: the first-century Jewish historian Josephus reports that Tyrian records, cited by earlier writers, mentioned Hiram and his dealings with Solomon. The mountains of Lebanon held great forests of cedar, prized for temples and palaces across the ancient world, and the kings of Egypt and Mesopotamia boasted of getting it. Sidonians is a general name here for the Phoenicians.

Solomon says that David could not build because of his wars. Chronicles gives another side of it, that David had shed much blood. Both explain why the son, and not the father, built the house.

Rest on every side is Deuteronomy's language. It promised that when God gave Israel rest from its enemies, he would choose a place for his name to dwell. The conditions for the temple are now met.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy had said that when the LORD ‘gives you rest from all the enemies around you and you dwell securely, then the LORD your God will choose a dwelling for His Name’ (Deuteronomy 12:10-11).

Chronicles remembers the word that came to David: ‘You have shed much blood and waged great wars. You are not to build a house for My Name’ (1 Chronicles 22:8).
passages.asks: Solomon began a great work because God had given rest. Ask what rest God has given you, and what it is for. And ask what promise of God you are waiting on that someone after you may be the one to see kept.

passages.t: Cedar for wheat, and a treaty
passages.happening:
Hiram is glad, and he praises the LORD for giving David a wise son over this great people (verse 7). He agrees to do all Solomon wants with the cedar and cypress. His servants will bring the logs down from Lebanon to the sea, float them as rafts to the place Solomon names and break them up there, and in exchange Solomon will provide food for Hiram's household (verses 8-9).

“So Hiram provided Solomon with all the cedar and cypress timber he wanted” (verse 10), and every year Solomon sent Hiram twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty thousand baths of pure olive oil (verse 11). “And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as He had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is built as an exchange of messages between two kings, a form known from ancient royal letters. Solomon moves from theology to business: God's rest, God's promise, then the request for cedar. Hiram answers with praise of the LORD and then terms of trade.

The trade suited both kingdoms. Phoenicia's narrow coast had timber and ships but little farmland; Israel had grain and olives. Chronicles names the port where the rafts came ashore as Joppa, and from there the timber was carried up to Jerusalem.

Verse 12 is the hinge of the chapter. It sets side by side two things the reader is meant to see together: the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he had promised, and there was peace and a treaty with Hiram.

A foreign king praises the LORD here. Later, at the temple, Solomon will pray for the foreigner who comes because of God's name (8:41-43).
passages.later:
Chronicles gives Hiram's promise in full: ‘we will float them to you as rafts by sea down to Joppa. Then you can take them up to Jerusalem’ (2 Chronicles 2:16).

Long afterward, Tyre and Sidon still depended on the land of Israel for their food. In Acts they ask King Herod for peace, ‘because their region depended on the king’s country for food’ (Acts 12:20).
passages.asks: Two kings met each other's needs, timber for food, and made peace. Ask what you have to offer a neighbor, and what you need from one. And ask whether your work for God has room for people who do not share your faith but are glad to help.

passages.happening:
“Then King Solomon conscripted a labor force of 30,000 men from all Israel” (verse 13). He sends them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand, one month in Lebanon and two at home, under Adoniram, who was in charge of the forced labor (verse 14). He also has seventy thousand porters and eighty thousand stonecutters in the hills, with 3,300 foremen over them (verses 15-16).

At the king's command they quarry ‘large, costly stones to lay the foundation of the temple with dressed stones’ (verse 17). Solomon's builders and Hiram's, with the men of Gebal, cut the stone and prepare the timber for the house (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Building a temple was the highest act of a king in that world. Royal inscriptions often say that a god gave the king rest from his enemies and that the king then built or restored the god's house, often with timber from Lebanon. Solomon's work fits that pattern, with one difference: his is a house for the Name of the LORD. In Deuteronomy, God's Name dwelling in a place means his real presence and ownership, while the God of heaven cannot be held by a building (8:27).

Forced labor, a set amount of work owed to the king each year, was common in the ancient world. Solomon's rotation softened it, one month away and two at home, but the numbers were huge. Chapter 9 says that Solomon made the remaining Canaanite peoples permanent slave labor and did not enslave Israelites, while this chapter describes a levy drawn from all Israel. Many interpreters distinguish permanent slavery for the Canaanite peoples from temporary service for Israelites. Either way, the resentment over this burden is what the northern tribes bring to Solomon's son in chapter 12.

The men of Gebal came from the Phoenician city the Greeks called Byblos.
passages.later:
The Hebrew word for this labor force, mas, is the word used for Egypt's work gangs: ‘So the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor’ (Exodus 1:11).

Joshua had already recorded Canaanites made forced laborers in the land: ‘So the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites to this day, but they are forced laborers’ (Joshua 16:10).
passages.asks: The house of God was built by the labor of tired men far from home. Ask whether the good things you build cost others more than you see. And ask how you would answer if the people who carry the load asked you to lighten it.
